text:
### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, every case ran the always-present activities A15, A17 and A18 early (mean position about 39–40% into the case), then A20 (about 46%) and A24 (about 65%), and finished with one of the three conditional activities A14, A16 or A19 near the end (about 68–69% into the case). In the later window this is reversed: the conditional activity runs early (about 34–35%), followed by A20 (about 38%) and A24 (about 57%), while A15, A17 and A18 run last (about 64%). [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, POS006, POS007, POS008]

- Ordering relations flip completely rather than partially: in all 21 recorded activity pairs the order is unanimous within each window and reverses between windows — for example, A15 preceded A20 in 100 of 100 earlier cases but in 0 of 100 later cases, A24 preceded A15 in 0 of 100 earlier cases but 100 of 100 later cases, and A16 moved from running after A24 (38 of 100 cases) to before it (29 of 100). A20 and A24 kept their mutual order in both windows. [REL001, REL008, REL009, REL013, REL015, REL020, POS007, POS008]

- Step distances change exactly as this reversal implies: the gap from A24 to A25 was 2 steps in all 200 earlier cases and 4 steps in all 200 later cases, and the gap from A35 to A20 was 4 steps earlier and 2 steps later — consistent with the three-activity segment A15/A17/A18 moving from before A20 to after A24, and the single conditional activity moving from after A24 to before A20. [LAG001, LAG002, POS002, POS005]

- Participation of the conditional alternatives also shifted: A14 ran in about 31 of 100 cases before and about 44 of 100 after (62 vs 87 of 200 traces), A16 fell from about 38 to about 29 in 100 (75 vs 57), and A19 from about 32 to about 28 in 100 (63 vs 56). Together the three account for about one execution per case in both windows, and A14 never repeats within a case. [OCC001, POS001, POS003, POS006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a reordering in which two segments exchanged their places around an unchanged middle: in the earlier window the always-executed segment A15–A17–A18 ran between A35 and A20 while a single conditional activity (one of A14, A16 or A19 per case) ran between A24 and A25; in the later window the conditional activity runs between A35 and A20 and A15, A17 and A18 run between A24 and A25, with A20 before A24 throughout and A35 and A25 keeping their sides. [POS002, POS004, POS007, POS008, REL008, REL009, LAG001, LAG002]

The support is direct and consistent: all 21 qualifying order relations reverse unanimously, both step-distance changes hold in every one of the 200 cases per window, and 32 control-flow items qualified against roughly 0.32 expected for an unchanged process — about 100 times the chance expectation — with each item's difference exceeding 199 of 200 random re-splits. [REL001, REL008, REL015, LAG001, LAG002]

Limitations: the evidence shows the net rearrangement but cannot distinguish one coordinated exchange of the two segments from two separate relocations, and because positions and distances are event-order measures, nothing can be inferred about clock-time timing. [LAG001, POS001]

Other differences: the choice among the three conditional alternatives shifted toward A14 (from about 31 to about 44 of 100 cases) at the expense of A16 (about 38 to 29) and A19 (about 32 to 28); this routing shift sits on top of the relocation and is not explained by it, though the A19 change (63 vs 56 of 200 traces) is small enough that sampling variation cannot be ruled out for it. [OCC001, POS001, POS003, POS006]
